function.name: run_in_terminal
function.description:
This tool allows you to execute shell commands in a persistent bash terminal session, preserving environment variables, working directory, and other context across multiple commands.

Command Execution:
- Use && to chain simple commands on one line
- Prefer pipelines | over temporary files for data flow
- Never create a sub-shell (eg. bash -c "command") unless explicitly asked

Directory Management:
- Prefer relative paths when navigating directories, only use absolute when the path is far away or the current cwd is not expected
- By default (mode=sync), shell and cwd are reused by subsequent sync commands
- Use $PWD for current directory references
- Consider using pushd/popd for directory stack management
- Supports directory shortcuts like ~ and -

Program Execution:
- Supports Python, Node.js, and other executables
- Install packages via package managers (brew, apt, etc.)
- Use which or command -v to verify command availability

Execution Mode:
- For ALL one-shot commands (builds, tests, installs, compilation, linting, downloads, scripts), use mode='sync' and omit timeout. The tool waits for the command to complete and returns full output inline. This is the default and strongly preferred mode.
- Use mode='async' ONLY for processes that must keep running indefinitely while you do other work (servers, watchers, dev daemons). Async waits for an initial idle/output signal, then returns a terminal ID and output snapshot while the process continues running.
- In sync mode, the full output is returned when the command completes — you do NOT need to call get_terminal_output afterward. Only use get_terminal_output if the tool result explicitly says the command was moved to background, timed out, or needs input.

Use send_to_terminal to send commands or input to a terminal session.

Output Management:
- Output exceeding 20KB is saved to a temp file; the result includes the file path so you can read the full output with readFile or search it with grep
- Use head, tail, grep, awk to filter and limit output size
- For pager commands, disable paging: git --no-pager or add | cat
- Use wc -l to count lines before displaying large outputs

Best Practices:
- Quote variables: "$var" instead of $var to handle spaces
- Use find with -exec or xargs for file operations
- Be specific with commands to avoid excessive output
- Avoid printing credentials unless absolutely required
- Avoid commands that require interactive privilege escalation, such as sudo/su/doas without a non-interactive flag (e.g. sudo -n). They block on a password prompt that cannot be answered in this mode, and secrets must never be routed through the model. If a command needs elevated privileges, tell the user to run it themselves in the terminal and stop — do NOT retry the command with variations.
- NEVER run sleep or similar wait commands in a terminal. You will be automatically notified on your next turn when async terminal commands or timed-out sync commands complete or need input. Do NOT poll for completion.
- NEVER pipe interactive commands through tail, head, grep, or other filters — this hides prompts and prevents the terminal from detecting when input is needed. Run interactive commands without pipes.

Interactive Input Handling:
- When a terminal command is waiting for interactive input, do NOT suggest alternatives or ask the user whether to proceed. Instead, use the vscode_askQuestions tool to collect the needed values from the user, then send them.
- NEVER use vscode_askQuestions to request sensitive input such as passwords, passphrases, API keys, tokens, or other secrets — answers to that tool are sent through the model. If the prompt requires a secret, tell the user to type it directly into the terminal and stop; do not call vscode_askQuestions or send_to_terminal for that prompt.
- Send exactly one answer per prompt using send_to_terminal. Never send multiple answers in a single send.
- After each send, call get_terminal_output to read the next prompt before sending the next answer.
- Continue one prompt at a time until the command finishes.
- Use [[ ]] for conditional tests instead of [ ]
- Prefer $() over backticks for command substitution

Execution mode:
- mode='sync' (strongly preferred): waits for the command to complete and returns full output inline. Use for ALL one-shot commands (builds, tests, installs, compilation, scripts). Omit timeout to let the command run to completion — the tool handles idle detection and input prompts automatically.
- mode='async': waits for an initial idle/output signal from the command, then returns a terminal ID and output snapshot while the process continues running. Use ONLY for processes that must keep running indefinitely (servers, watchers, daemons). Timeout caps how long to wait for the initial idle/output signal.

Timeout parameter: Usually omit timeout entirely for sync commands — the tool returns automatically on completion, input-needed, or cancellation. Only set a timeout as a safety net for commands you suspect might hang. Use 0 to explicitly indicate no timeout.

Sync output is final: When a sync command completes, the full output is returned inline — do NOT call get_terminal_output afterward. Only use get_terminal_output if the tool result explicitly indicates the command was moved to background, timed out, or needs input. Do NOT tell the user to check the terminal panel — all command output is already included in the tool result.

Terminal notifications: When an async command finishes or a sync command times out, you will be automatically notified on your next turn with the exit code and terminal output. You will also be notified if the terminal needs input. Do NOT poll or sleep to wait for completion.

goal.description: A short description of the goal or purpose of the command (e.g., "Install dependencies", "Start development server").

enumDescriptions: Wait for command completion and return full output inline. Strongly preferred for all one-shot commands (builds, tests, installs, scripts).

Wait for an initial idle/output signal, then return a terminal ID and output snapshot while the process continues running. Timeout caps how long to wait for the initial signal. Use ONLY for processes that must keep running indefinitely (servers, watchers, daemons).

Commands: "traceValue" — walk the program flow graph backwards from a position to explain how a variable got its value (assignments, narrowing, try/except). Use when the user asks "where does this value come from?" or "what does this depend on?". "typeAt" — get the inferred/narrowed Python type at a position (lighter than `pylanceLSP textDocument/hover`, returns only the type). "flowGraph" — return an ASCII visualization of the code-flow graph at a position; useful for debugging unexpected narrowing or branch behavior. "traceFailure" — trace value provenance across multiple stack frames (caller-supplied, innermost-first); bridges through function-parameter boundaries by resolving the matching argument at each call site. "tracePytestFailure" — paste raw pytest failure output and the tool extracts frames, assertions, and variables automatically and runs traceFailure for each failure. "help" — full per-command parameter reference. Prefer `pylanceLSP textDocument/definition` for "where is this defined?"; use this tool for value provenance across reassignments and conditions, not symbol resolution. Positions are LSP 0-based `{ line, character }`; URIs must be `file://` and inside the workspace.

function.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceInvokeRefactoring
function.description:
Apply named Pylance refactorings to a Python file, including unused-import cleanup, import-format/star/module conversion, inferred type annotations, shadowed-stdlib import renames, and fix-all. Prefer this over hand edits for these operations because Pylance uses symbol and import resolution that text rewrites cannot safely reconstruct. Modes: "update" applies edits, "edits" previews a WorkspaceEdit, and "string" returns updated content; default is "update". Available refactorings: source.unusedImports: - Removes all unused import statements from a Python file. Use when imports are imported but never referenced in the code. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with unused imports.
source.optionalMemberAccessAssert: - Inserts assert statements like `assert x is not None` before statements that access members on optional receivers. Use when optional member access diagnostics should be narrowed automatically across a file. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with optional member access diagnostics.
source.convertImportFormat: - Converts import statements between absolute and relative formats according to python.analysis.importFormat setting. Use when import format consistency is needed. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with imports to convert.
source.convertImportStar: - Converts all wildcard imports (from module import *) to explicit imports listing all imported symbols. Use when explicit imports are preferred for better code clarity and IDE support. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with wildcard imports.
source.convertImportToModule: - Converts `from module import name1, name2` (including wildcard imports) into `import module` and rewrites references to `module.name1`, `module.name2`. Use when you want module-qualified references. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with `from ... import ...` statements.
source.renameShadowedStdlibImports: - Renames imported user modules that shadow standard library module names (e.g. a local calendar.py). Use to avoid import shadowing bugs. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to the importing Python file.
source.addTypeAnnotation: - Adds type annotations to all variables and functions in a Python file that can be inferred from their usage. Use when type hints are needed for better type checking and code clarity. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with unannotated variables or functions.
source.fixAll.pylance: - Applies all available automatic code fixes from python.analysis.fixAll setting. Use when multiple code issues need to be addressed simultaneously. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with fixable issues.
workspace.generateDependencies: - Analyzes Python imports in the workspace and generates or updates a dependency file (requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, requirements.in, environment.yml). Use when you need to create or update dependency files based on actual code imports. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to the workspace root. Optional parameters: format ("requirements.txt" | "pyproject.toml" | "pyproject.toml-poetry" | "requirements.in" | "environment.yml" | "auto"), versionPin ("exact" | "compatible" | "none"), syncMode (boolean to remove stale deps).

This must be one of these [source.unusedImports, source.optionalMemberAccessAssert, source.convertImportFormat, source.convertImportStar, source.convertImportToModule, source.renameShadowedStdlibImports, source.addTypeAnnotation, source.fixAll.pylance, workspace.generateDependencies]

mode.description: Determines the output mode: "update" updates the file directly, "edits" returns a WorkspaceEdit, "string" returns the updated content as a string. If omitted, "update" will be used as the default. The "edits" mode is especially useful for checking if any changes are needed (such as unused imports or import formatting issues) without modifying the file, as it will return a WorkspaceEdit only if edits are required.

function.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceLSP
function.description: Read-only Pylance/Pyright LSP access for Python using the workspace editor state and selected interpreter. Use for cross-file Python code intelligence: find all references to a function/class, rename-impact analysis, every caller/call site, call hierarchy, definitions, document/workspace symbols, hover/type/signature info, and Pylance diagnostics. Parameters follow LSP: file paths are `file:///...` URIs; positions and ranges are 0-based `{ line, character }`; most textDocument methods need `{ textDocument: { uri }, position: { line, character } }`. Diagnostics: use `textDocument/diagnostic` for one file and read each `Diagnostic.code` for the exact `reportXxx` Pylance rule, such as `reportArgumentType` or `reportOptionalMemberAccess`, before explaining or fixing any reported error. It takes `{ textDocument: { uri } }` and returns `{ kind: "full", items: Diagnostic[] }`. Use `workspace/diagnostic` with `{}` to enumerate diagnostics across the whole workspace in one call when the user wants project-wide errors instead of walking files; its response is `{ items: [{ uri, kind: "full", items: Diagnostic[] }, ...] }`, so inspect every returned file entry. Include diagnostic messages, severities, codes, and ranges when the user asks about Pylance problems. Relationships: use `textDocument/references` for rename impact analysis and all usages, including aliased/re-exported call sites. Use `callHierarchy/prepare` then `callHierarchy/incomingCalls` or `callHierarchy/outgoingCalls` to trace callers, callees, or bug propagation across functions. Use type hierarchy for class ancestry. Navigation and facts: use `textDocument/definition`, `declaration`, `typeDefinition`, or `implementation` for targets; use `textDocument/hover` and `textDocument/signatureHelp` for inferred types and call parameters; use `textDocument/documentSymbol` or `workspace/symbol` to enumerate symbols; use highlights, inlay hints, semantic tokens, code lens, folding, colors, and selections when those exact editor facts are requested. For requirements.txt or dependency audits, prefer `pylanceImports` plus `pylanceInstalledTopLevelModules`; use diagnostics only when locations, severities, exact rule codes, or workspace problem lists matter. Use method `help` for the full 31-method reference with exact parameters, response shapes, and less-common methods.

function.name: activate_prisma_migrate_development
function.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group consists of two Prisma Migrate tools designed for managing database schema migrations during development. The `prisma-migrate-dev` tool is used to synchronize the database schema with the Prisma schema file (`schema.prisma`). It performs a multi-step process: first, it re-runs existing migrations in a shadow database to detect any drift caused by manual edits or deleted migration files; second, it applies any pending migrations from colleagues; third, it generates a new migration from recent schema changes; fourth, it applies all unapplied migrations to the development database; and finally, it triggers artifact generation (e.g., Prisma Client). The complementary tool, `prisma-migrate-reset`, is used to forcefully reset the database and migration history when drift is detected or a clean slate is needed. It drops the database (or performs a soft reset if dropping is not possible), creates a new schema, applies all migrations, and runs seed scripts. This reset tool should only be used on development databases and never on production. Together, these tools enable a smooth development workflow where schema changes can be iterated and validated quickly, with the ability to start fresh when migration history becomes inconsistent.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

function.name: activate_prisma_platform_setup
function.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group contains tools for setting up and managing online Prisma Postgres databases via the Prisma Platform. The `prisma-platform-login` tool handles authentication by logging in an existing user or creating a new account, which is a prerequisite for using Prisma Postgres services. The `prisma-postgres-create-database` tool allows the creation of a new online Postgres database, requiring a user-specified name and a region selection from a list that includes us-east-1, eu-west-3, ap-northeast-1, ap-southeast-1, or by calling without a region to get updated options. If the workspace plan limit is reached, the tool returns guidance: the user can either connect to an existing database via the Prisma Console (console.prisma.io) to obtain a connection string, upgrade their plan, or delete unused databases. These tools work sequentially: first ensure the user is logged in, then create the database in an appropriate region. They are essential for initializing a Prisma Postgres environment for development or production use.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

Prisma Migrate Dev is used to update Prisma whenever the schema.prisma file has been modified.
Use this tool instead of running `prisma migrate dev` on the CLI.
Always provide a descriptive name argument describing the change that was made to the Prisma Schema.
The migrate dev command performs these steps:
1. Reruns the existing migration history in the shadow database in order to detect schema drift (edited or deleted migration file, or a manual changes to the database schema)
2. Applies pending migrations to the shadow database (for example, new migrations created by colleagues)
3. Generates a new migration from any changes you made to the Prisma schema before running migrate dev
4. Applies all unapplied migrations to the development database and updates the _prisma_migrations table
5. Triggers the generation of artifacts (for example, Prisma Client)

Create a new online Prisma Postgres database.
Specify a name that makes sense to the user - maybe the name of the project they are working on.
Specify a region that makes sense for the user. Pick between these options: us-east-1, eu-west-3, ap-northeast-1, ap-southeast-1 or call the tool without a region to get an up-to-date list of available regions. If you are unsure, pick us-east-1.

If they want to connect to an existing database, they should go to console.prisma.io and copy the connection string
If they want to upgrade their plan, they should go to console.prisma.io and upgrade their plan in order to be able to create more databases
If they want to delete a database they no longer need, they should go to console.prisma.io and delete the database project.
If the user is not logged in, you should suggest them to login via the `prisma-platform-login` tool.
